title: Choosing Day

beats.what: Jade wakes up from the car crash in straps; dismisses the entire situation as an elaborate escape-room stunt
Frank is told his punishment is a night in the box with no talisman; Boyd admits he built the box as a deterrent he never intended to use
Father Khatri explains the Choosing Day ceremony to Jim and Tabitha; the town and Colony House as permanent factions
Boyd and Khatri argue over whether to actually put Frank in the box; Khatri invokes the guillotine metaphor
Victor reveals to Ethan he is checking whether the trees have moved; says they are four inches closer
Frank addresses the gathered town, confesses he let the place get into his head, then chooses the box voluntarily
Julie chooses Colony House at the ceremony, splitting the family
Jade finally confronts reality when he sees Tobey's body; his escape-room theory collapses

character_beats.beat: Wants to uphold the rule of the box to preserve social order yet cannot bring himself to enforce it; resolution comes only when Frank removes the choice from him
Wants the entire situation to be an elaborate prank and performs that belief through the whole episode until the body breaks it
Wants autonomy and is done being treated as the child who makes wrong decisions; chooses Colony House as an act of self-assertion even if it hurts her family

key_lines.line: You built a guillotine in the town square. What happens when people realize you lack the conviction to use it?
key_lines.why: Khatri names the structural trap Boyd is caught in; the logic of deterrence requires follow-through

key_lines.line: I let this town, those things in the woods, I let them get to my head.
key_lines.why: Frank's confession articulates how the place destroys people from the inside, not only outside

key_lines.line: I'm checking to see if they've moved. The trees.
key_lines.why: Victor's obsessive tree-measurement is the first sign the town's geography is actively changing

key_lines.line: There is a fine line between savagery and consequence.
key_lines.why: Boyd's framing of the box problem in public sets up his private inability to act

open_loops: Are the trees physically closing in on the town?
What is the mysterious boy Ethan sees who Victor says hello to?
How long has Victor been in the town and what does he actually know?
What did Sara do that led to an incident before the newcomers arrived?
Will Julie's choice to live apart from her family hold?

payoffs.what: The 'man protects his family' phrase echoes in Frank's confession that he failed his family by letting the town break him
The talisman rule explained in E02 becomes the source of the punishment logic: no talisman in the box means death

contradiction.wants: To be a fair leader who maintains order without cruelty
contradiction.does: Built a torture device and is now forced to use it or lose authority; chooses to enforce it only because Frank volunteers

tone_notes: The episode's longest silence is 97 seconds (05:02-06:40), the title card and song gap. A second silence of 50 seconds (51:13-52:03) closes the episode after Frank enters the box, the longest dead-quiet ending in the batch. Density is highest at minutes 17-22 (100-174 w/min), matching the Boyd-Khatri argument. The Jade scenes punctuate with dark comedy at low-density pockets, functioning as tonal relief before the Frank sequence tightens.
